newsitem.title: USA: ABA refuses to take stand on doctor-assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: ABA refuses to take stand on doctor-assisted suicide.

text.p: The American Bar Association refused on Wednesday to take a stand on doctor-assisted suicide, voting that the matter be left to state legislatures.
In adopting the innocuous proposal, the ABA shied away from becoming embroiled in a controversial issue that some members warned could result in a drop in membership and hurt the bar's public image.

The issue had pitted more conservative members of the ABA against those who felt it was the ABA's duty to take positions on key legal issues of the day, despite the effect it might have on the association.

A similar situation occurred when the ABA debated whether to take a position on abortion. A number of members withdrew from the organisation after it voted to oppose legislation that would restrict a woman's right to have an abortion.

Indeed, some members were so worried about taking any action on doctor-assisted suicide that they urged that the ABA delay a vote on the proposal, which basically followed a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in June.
"Why should we worry about this? Why are we marching down the road I call the death march ... are we on a death march to ruin our organisation?" said Frank Bazler of Troy, Ohio.
F. William McCalpin, a St. Louis lawyer speaking on behalf of the Senior Lawyers Division that submitted the proposal, assured colleagues "It is not authorising a license to kill."
"This resolution takes no position on whether or not physician-assisted suicide is desirable, needed or should be considered," he said.

The proposal approved by the ABA said that if a state or territory passed laws allowing doctor-assisted suicide it should ensure that information and reporting systems were established to closely monitor the impact of such practices.

The Beverly Hills Bar Association had planned to submit a controversial proposal suggesting the ABA support legislation that would allow doctor-assisted suicide, and the matter had been scheduled to be debated Wednesday.

But late on Tuesday, when the group realised it could not win, it revised the proposal and submitted a watered-down version. Even that proposal was dropped on Wednesday in favour of the one submitted by the Senior Lawyers Division.

Daniel McIntosh, president of the Beverly Hills Bar, told the lawyers he realised many ABA members were uncomfortable with its original proposal, but as the largest and most powerful law organisation in the nation the ABA had a duty to take positions.
He said doctors were currently helping people die, but it was usually just the rich who had this option. McIntosh said it was time to bring the issue "out of the shadow and into the light."
"We need to provide guidance and leadership on this issue," he said.
The ABA vote comes shortly after the Supreme Court ruled in June that states have the right to pass laws concerning the practice and can act to ban it entirely.

It also comes as Oregon residents gear up for a November referendum challenging a 1994 initiative that allows doctor-assisted suicides. Oregon is the only state to have passed such a proposal, but the law has been on hold because of litigation.
